Weaknesses:

[1] Attributable visual similarity learning.

[2] Deep Relational Metric Learning.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Contextual similarity and contrastive learning are jointly considered in similarity measurement and regularization. The authors provide some theories to validate their claims. Some experiments on image retrieval show the effectiveness of the proposed method, especially when using the Recall@1 metric.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 
Contextual similarity and cosine function are combined into a contextual cosine similarity measurement. Moreover, the corresponding discrete optimization is developed to circumvent the non-differential cases. A simple similarity regularize is also developed to improve its performance. The authors present some theories to support their claims, and the experiments show its efficacy of the proposed method on image retrieval.

Weaknesses
1. The reviewer wonders if we directly use other distance metrics rather than cosine distance, whether the proposed method will work? Could it be extended to other similar cases? Does the optimization algorithm work well?
2. For context and regularization terms are used for defining and improving the discriminant of the representation. Meanwhile, contrastive loss can act as the same function. Which one is more important? Is it redundant? What are their different functions? To me, they have the same effects.
3. For image retrieval, we seldomly use only recall@topk as the main evaluation metric. By contrast, we usually employ the MAP@topk, Precision@topk, and PR curves, etc. If you only use the recall score, this is not fair.
4. For the used datasets, the authors are strongly recommended using large-scale datasets, rather than simple ones. Multi-label datasets are highly recommended. Moreover, more categories are also welcome, such as SUN397. The current experiments are not satisfactory.
5. For the codes, the authors claim to release their codes, but it is really hard to run them. For retrieval tasks, if your model is trained on a P100 or A100 GPU card, you should consume more than 12 hours. To me, it is not acceptable, although there are lots of works that are trained on 100 or more GPUs. Efficiency is more important than others when the accuracy is acceptable.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is clearly presented, yet the novelty is not well explored. Maybe, the proposed method is reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The general idea of this paper is easy to understand and some theoretic and experimental analyses could support their claims. However, whether is it really applicable or acceptable for research is hard to estimate.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the deep metric learning problem. Different from the existing literature on this topic, the paper develops a solution based on a proposed textual similarity loss together with contrastive loss and a similarity regularization loss. The major contribution is that the paper explicitly addresses the non-differentiability issues for contextual loss. The resulting loss function is evaluated against the state-of-the-art with four benchmark datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
-	the proposed loss function through contextual similarity is novel, in particular, in addressing the non-differentiability issues
-	the reported evaluations and the ablation studies are arguably extensive
-	the presentation is clear though there are grammatical errors
Weaknesses:
-	The evaluation results reported in table 1 are based on only three trials for each case. While this is fine, statistically this is not significant, and thus it does not make sense to report the deviations. That is why that in many cases the deviation is 0. Due to this reason, statements such as “our performance is at least two standard deviation better than the next best baseline” do not make sense.
-	In the reported ablation studies in Table 2, for CUB and SOP datasets, the complete loss function performed even worse than those with some terms missing. That does not appear to make sense. Why?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As I stated earlier, the presentation is clear though there are grammatical errors. From the presentation it appears that the method can be reproduced. The paper also has a statement promising to release data and code for facilitating reproducibility. Overall, the quality is acceptable.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work addresses the deep metric learning problem with a new approach focusing on textual similarity. The major contribution is the theoretical analysis to explicitly address the non-differentiability issues in the definition of contextual similarity. The empirical studies are arguably extensive and convincing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a metric learning framework where the goal is to optimize the contextualized similarity, which counts the number of neighbors of a sample, to compare with the ground truth labels while regularizing the overall distances. The authors also design some artifact gradients for discrete operators in order to optimize the counting numbers within the continuous space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

This paper introduces an interesting optimization goal that is different from the traditional DML goals. The loss is based on the contextual similarity proposed in [1], where the number of overlapping samples within the neighbors' range is counted. The optimization process also contains some novelty where authors propose some artifact gradient to get over the discrete operators.

[1] Kim, Sungyeon, et al. "Self-Taught Metric Learning without Labels." CVPR 2022



Weakness:

This paper is hard to follow due to its limited writing quality. Though the authors provide some figures, it's still difficult to understand how the similarity is defined and optimized. And the notations in section 3 are a mess and unclear. I believe the description in section 3 should be rewritten to make this paper easier to understand. 

The experimental results in table 1 are not convincing. The authors propose the results of SOTA that is not consistent with the published original paper. The authors claim that their results of R@1 outperform the SOTA on all benchmarks. However, this is not true. There are many SOTA works [1][2][3] or more under the same setting and backbones that the authors do not list for comparison, which is better than the results of R@1 the authors propose.

The ablation results in table 2 are not convincing. It seems the R@1 in Cars has higher results even without the context loss. Why does the best result on SOP also happen in the case without context loss? This is not consistent with the conclusion in section 5.1. Also, the contents in table 3 are uncleared or misleading. 


[1] Ebrahimpour et al. "Multi-Head Deep Metric Learning Using Global and Local Representations." CVPR 2022

[2] Zhang, Borui, et al. "Attributable Visual Similarity Learning." CVPR 2022

[3] Venkataramanan, Shashanka, et al. "It takes two to tango: Mixup for deep metric learning." ICLR 2022

content.title: Supervised Metric Learning for Retrieval via Contextual Similarity Optimization
content.abstract: Existing deep metric learning approaches fall into three general categories: contrastive learning, average precision (AP) maximization, and classification. We propose a novel alternative approach, contextual similarity optimization, inspired by work in unsupervised metric learning. Contextual similarity is a discrete similarity measure based on relationships between neighborhood sets, and is widely used in the unsupervised setting as pseudo-supervision. Inspired by this success, we propose a framework which optimizes a combination of contextual and cosine similarities. Contextual similarity calculation involves several non-differentiable operations, including the heaviside function and intersection of sets. We show how to circumvent non-differentiability to explicitly optimize contextual similarity, and we further incorporate appropriate similarity regularization to yield our novel metric learning loss. The resulting loss function achieves state-of-the-art Recall @ 1 accuracy on standard supervised image retrieval benchmarks when combined with the standard contrastive loss.
